Benchmark.title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Internal Only - General Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Internal Only - General Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completed successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Internal Only - General Target Technology Details This document provides prescriptive guidance for running Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) vNext following recommended security controls. This benchmark only includes controls which can be modified by an end user of OKE. For information on OKE's performance against the Kubernetes CIS benchmarks, for items which cannot be audited or modified, see the OKE documentation at https://docs.cloud.oracle.com/en- us/iaas/Content/ContEng/Concepts/contengoverview.htm To obtain the latest version of this guide, please visit www.cisecurity.org. If you have questions, comments, or have identified ways to improve this guide, please write us at support@cisecurity.org.

Rule.title: Use OCI IAM or OIDC tokens instead of user client certificates
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>OKE authenticates cluster users through OCI IAM by default, and enhanced clusters can also be configured to use an external OIDC identity provider for user authentication.
User access should rely on OCI IAM or OIDC tokens rather than Kubernetes client certificates, because these mechanisms align user access to managed identity, policy, and RBAC controls.
OKE provides a managed Kubernetes control plane, and control plane authentication settings are modified only through supported OKE APIs and configuration options.
Client certificates used by Kubernetes components are not a customer-managed user authentication method

Rationale:
With any authentication mechanism the ability to revoke credentials if they are compromised or no longer required, is a key control. OKE kubeconfig version 2.0.0 uses an OCI CLI command to dynamically generate short lived user-specific authentication tokens. These tokens are not intended to be shared between users, and OIDC can be used when the organization wants users to authenticate through an external identity provider.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Replace user kubeconfig entries that use client certificates with OCI IAM generated tokens or OIDC token based authentication. For OKE clusters, user authentication should align to the supported OKE access model, where OCI IAM is used by default and OIDC can be configured for external identity provider based authentication. This allows user access to be managed through identity, policy, and Kubernetes RBAC controls rather than long lived certificate material stored in kubeconfig files.
• For OCI IAM based access, regenerate the user kubeconfig file from OKE using kubeconfig token version 2.0.0 so the user entry uses the OCI CLI exec plugin to generate authentication tokens.
• For OIDC based access, configure the OKE cluster for OIDC authentication and update the user kubeconfig entry to use the approved OIDC identity provider token flow.
• Remove or replace any user kubeconfig entries that contain client- certificate, client-certificate-data, client-key, or client-key-dat a, then validate that required users can still authenticate with only their approved RBAC permissions.
Internal Only - General

check.check-content:
Review user access to the cluster and ensure that users are not making use of Kubernetes client certificate authentication.
Review approved user kubeconfig files and confirm that user entries use OCI IAM generated tokens or OIDC tokens instead of client certificate fields.
Run the following command to verify the authentication method configured for users in the current kubeconfig file:
Internal Only - General
kubectl config view --raw -o json | jq -r '
.users[]
| [
.name,
(
if .user.exec then "exec_token"
elif .user["auth-provider"]?.name == "oidc" then "oidc_token"
elif .user.token then "static_token"
elif (
.user["client-certificate"]? or
.user["client-certificate-data"]? or
.user["client-key"]? or
.user["client-key-data"]?
) then "client_certificate"
else "unknown"
end
)
]
| @tsv
'
The expected result is that user entries use exec_token for OCI IAM based OKE access or oidc_token for OIDC based access. Any user entry showing client_certificate should be reviewed and replaced with a supported OCI IAM or OIDC token based access method.

Rule.title: Ensure authorized access to OCI Audit logs for OKE activity
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>OCI Audit logs are separate from OKE managed Kubernetes control plane service logs.
OKE integrates with the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service to record operations performed by Kubernetes Engine and the Kubernetes API server as Audit log events.
Operations performed by Kubernetes Engine and the Kubernetes API server are visible as log events in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service.

Rationale:
Logging is a crucial detective control for all systems to detect potential unauthorized access. Authorized access to OCI Audit logs helps security and operations teams review OKE activity, identify security anomalies, support compliance checks, and troubleshoot errors by identifying who did what and when.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content: Update OCI IAM policies so only approved security, operations, or audit groups can read OCI Audit events for the required tenancy or compartment. Remove broad or unnecessary Audit access from users or groups that do not require it, and validate that authorized users can view OKE related events in the Audit service using the appropriate compartment and filters.

check.check-content:
To monitor and manage operations performed by Container Engine for Kubernetes on a particular cluster:
Review IAM policies and confirm that only authorized groups are granted access to read OCI Audit events for the tenancy or approved compartment. The read audit-events permission allows access to Audit log events.
To view operations performed by Container Engine for Kubernetes and the Kubernetes API server as log events in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service:
Open the navigation menu, select Identity & Security, and then select Audit. Choose the compartment you have permission to work in, then search and filter for the operations of interest. Use ClustersAPI to view operations performed by Kubernetes Engine, and use OKE API Server Admin Access to view operations performed by the Kubernetes API server.
Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Ensure that the kubelet.conf file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If kubelet is running, and if it is using a file-based kubelet.conf file, ensure that the proxy kubelet.conf file has permissions of 644 or more restrictive.

Rationale:
The kubelet kubelet.conf file controls various parameters of the kubelet service in the worker node. You should restrict its file permissions to maintain the integrity of the file.
The file should be writable by only the administrators on the system.
It is possible to run kubelet with the kubeconfig parameters configured as a Kubernetes ConfigMap instead of a file. In this case, there is no proxy kubelet.conf file.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Run the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker node. For example, Internal Only - General
chmod 644 <kubelet.conf file>

check.check-content:
Method 1 Optional: Run the following command to enter debug mode where NODE_NAME and IMAGE are defined variables:
kubectl debug node/$NODE_NAME -it --image=$IMAGE --profile=general
Run the following command on each node to find the appropriate kubeconfig file:
ps -efww | grep kubelet | grep -- '--kubeconfig'
The command line output should show a path for kubeconfig similar to -- kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf which is the location of the kubeconfig file.
Run this command to obtain the kubeconfig file permissions:
Internal Only - General
stat -c %a /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf (or stat -c %a
/host/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf if in debub mode)
The output of the above command gives you the kubeconfig file's permissions.
Verify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive.
Method 2 Create and Run a Privileged Pod.
You will need to run a pod that is privileged enough to access the host's file system.
This can be achieved by deploying a pod that uses the hostPath volume to mount the node's file system into the pod.
Here's an example of a simple pod definition that mounts the root of the host to /host within the pod:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: file-check
spec:
volumes:
- name: host-root
hostPath:
path: /
type: Directory
containers:
- name: nsenter
image: busybox
command: ["sleep", "3600"]
volumeMounts:
- name: host-root
mountPath: /host
securityContext:
privileged: true
Save this to a file (e.g., file-check-pod.yaml) and create the pod:
kubectl apply -f file-check-pod.yaml
Once the pod is running, you can exec into it to check file permissions on the node:
kubectl exec -it -n kube-public file-check -- sh
Now you are in a shell inside the pod, but you can access the node's file system through the /host directory and check the permission level of the file:
ls -l /host/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
Verify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive.

Rule.title: Ensure kubelet anonymous authentication is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In Oracle OKE, this control means the kubelet on managed or self managed worker nodes must not accept unauthenticated requests. OKE worker nodes run kubelet to communicate with the cluster control plane, and kubelet behavior can be configured through supported worker node startup or provisioning configuration. This requirement is represented by disabling kubelet anonymous authentication rather than relying only on a process list check for --anonymous-auth=false.

Rationale:
The kubelet exposes node local functionality on each applicable worker node, and Kubernetes documents that requests not rejected by other configured authentication methods are otherwise treated as system:anonymous in the system:unauthenticated group. The KubeletConfiguration schema defines authentication.anonymous.enabled as the setting that controls this behavior, so the technically correct review point in OKE is the effective kubelet configuration on each applicable managed or self managed worker node.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
If the audit returns true, the worker node is allowing anonymous requests to the kubelet and should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is null or the field is missing, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies that endpoint as the view of the kubelet’s final effective configuration. Once the result is validated, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported worker node provisioning or node update workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. OKE supports custom cloud-init scripts for managed nodes, and the corrected setting should be applied by creating, cycling, or replacing worker nodes.
Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node pool, the goal is to ensure worker nodes join the cluster with kubelet anonymous authentication already disabled. This is done by defining the setting in the worker node startup or provisioning configuration that OKE applies during node creation.
• Define kubelet anonymous authentication as disabled in the worker node startup or provisioning configuration before nodes join the cluster
• For managed nodes, update the custom cloud-init script so the OKE initialization script passes --anonymous-auth=false through --kubelet-extra-args, then replace or cycle the worker nodes so the setting is applied at node startup.
Internal Only - General
• Validate the live effective kubelet configuration after deployment to confirm the setting resolves to false.
Remediation of existing running cluster For an existing OKE cluster, the objective is to change the node pool or provisioning configuration and then replace the current nodes so the corrected kubelet setting is applied consistently across the node pool. This ensures the fix is durable and survives restart, scale out, and node replacement events.
• Update the custom cloud-init script or equivalent node provisioning configuration so the effective kubelet setting disables anonymous authentication.
• Apply the updated configuration to the managed node pool or self managed node build process.
• Replace, cycle, or rebuild the existing worker nodes, then re-audit the replacement nodes using the live kubelet configuration to confirm the effective value is false.
Note: Even though it is tempting to do so, direct edits to the kubelet config file on OKE worker nodes are discouraged because they can be overwritten, may not match the live effective kubelet configuration, and can be lost when nodes are replaced, rebuilt, or recycled.

check.check-content:
To audit whether kubelet anonymous authentication is disabled on an Oracle OKE worker node, query the live kubelet configuration through the Kubernetes API server proxy and inspect the configz output. This is preferred over relying only on the kubelet process list because kubelet settings can be applied through startup configuration, configuration files, or command line arguments.
Using the API configz endpoint search for the status of authentication...
"anonymous":{"enabled":false} by extracting the live configuration from the nodes running kubelet.
Set the local proxy port and the following variables and provide proxy port number and node name; HOSTNAME_PORT="localhost-and-port-number" NODE_NAME="The- Name-Of-Node-To-Extract-Configuration" from the output of kubectl get nodes Internal Only - General
kubectl proxy --port=8001 &
export HOSTNAME_PORT=localhost:8001 (example host and port number)
export NODE_NAME=10.0.10.180 (example node name from "kubectl get nodes")
curl -sSL "http://${HOSTNAME_PORT}/api/v1/nodes/${NODE_NAME}/proxy/configz"
or
curl -sSL "http://${HOSTNAME_PORT}/api/v1/nodes/${NODE_NAME}/proxy/configz" |
jq (for a more readable output)
Output should show something similar to "authentication"..."anonymous":{"enabled":false} in the output.
To interpret the result:
• false = Pass. Anonymous requests to the kubelet are disabled. Kubernetes states that disabling anonymous access causes unauthenticated requests to receive 401 Unauthorized.
• true = Fail. Requests not rejected by another authentication method can be treated as system:anonymous in the system:unauthenticated group.
• null or missing = Investigate further. That would be unexpected for a normal kubelet config response because authentication.anonymous is part of the kubelet configuration structure; verify that the request reached the kubelet successfully and that you are querying the intended node.

Rule.title: Ensure kubelet authorization mode is set to Webhook
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In OKE, the available kubelet authorization modes are AlwaysAllow and Webhook. For worker nodes, the recommended setting is Webhook, which uses the Kubernetes authorization flow to evaluate access to the kubelet API. In contrast, AlwaysAllow is not optimal because it bypasses that authorization decision and permits kubelet requests without a webhook-based access check. For OKE managed nodes, kubelet configuration should be validated from the effective node configuration and maintained through the supported worker node initialization and node pool update process.

Rationale:
Oracle documents that OKE managed nodes can use custom cloud-init initialization scripts and that the OKE default initialization logic should not be modified. Custom logic, including supported kubelet extra arguments, should be added before or after that default logic so worker nodes are built consistently when they join the cluster. In that model, the technically correct target is the effective kubelet configuration on the node, with authorization.mode set to Webhook instead of an unrestricted mode such as AlwaysAllow.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
If the audit returns AlwaysAllow, the worker node is permitting kubelet requests without webhook-based authorization and should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is null or the field is missing, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies that endpoint as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration. Once the result is validated, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported worker node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. Oracle documents that OKE managed nodes can use custom cloud-init initialization scripts, that the OKE default logic should not be modified, and that worker node property changes apply to new worker nodes.
Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node group, the goal is to ensure worker nodes join the cluster with kubelet authorization already set to Webhook. This is done by defining the setting in the worker node initialization configuration that OKE applies during node creation.
• Define kubelet authorization mode as Webhook in the worker node initialization configuration so the setting is present when nodes first join the cluster.

export NODE_NAME=10.0.10.4 # example node name from kubectl get nodes

Rule.title: Ensure the kubelet client certificate rotation is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In OKE, the setting rotateCertificates is about whether the kubelet renews its client certificate before that certificate expires. Oracle OKE documentation shows worker nodes using the kubelet client certificate at /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client- current.pem, which is trusted by the cluster CA, but Oracle does not publish a fixed OKE default for rotateCertificates. In practice, that means true is the recommended operational state for long-lived nodes, while false or a not present setting should be treated as rotation not enabled unless OKE is explicitly managing the certificate lifecycle for that worker node configuration.
In addition, rotateCertificates should be not be confused with a similar setting 'RotateKubeletServerCertificate'. Client certificate rotation affects the certificate the kubelet uses when it authenticates to the Kubernetes API server. By contrast, RotateKubeletServerCertificate refers to the kubelet’s serving certificate, which is the certificate the kubelet presents from its own HTTPS endpoint when another component connects to it. Oracle OKE documentation also distinguishes client certificate usage from CA validation by showing the kubelet client certificate and key used to authenticate to a worker node metrics endpoint, and the cluster root CA used to verify the server certificate presented by that endpoint.

Rationale:
Enabling kubelet client certificate rotation allows the kubelet to automatically generate a new key and submit a new certificate signing request through the Kubernetes API before its current client certificate expires. Oracle OKE documentation shows that required certificates are available on worker nodes after provisioning and identifies /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem as the kubelet client certificate trusted by the cluster CA. Oracle does not document a fixed rotateCertificates default for OKE, so the effective kubelet configuration should be verified directly. In practical terms, a setting of true means the kubelet is configured to renew its client certificate, while false or not present should be interpreted conservatively as rotation not enabled unless the platform is explicitly managing certificate renewal for you.
This setting is distinct from RotateKubeletServerCertificate. Client certificate rotation protects the certificate the node uses to authenticate to the API server, while server certificate rotation separately governs the certificate the kubelet presents from its HTTPS endpoint to callers.
Internal Only - General</VulnDiscussion>

If the audit returns false, the worker node is not configured to rotate its kubelet client certificate and should be treated as noncompliant. If the field is not present, interpret that conservatively as rotation not enabled unless your OKE platform explicitly manages certificate rotation for you. Oracle OKE documentation shows worker nodes using kubelet client certificates trusted by the cluster CA and supports managed node customization through cloud-init initialization scripts and kubelet extra args. Oracle also documents that worker node property changes can be applied through new or replacement managed nodes.
Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node pool, the goal is to ensure worker nodes start with kubelet client certificate rotation enabled if the nodes may remain in service long enough for certificate expiry to matter. In OKE, this should be applied through the supported managed node initialization path rather than as a host-level edit, because Oracle supports custom cloud-init initialization scripts and kubelet extra args for managed nodes.
• Set rotateCertificates: true in the worker node’s kubelet configuration.
• Use a custom cloud-init initialization script when this setting must be enforced at node creation.
• Apply the setting through the supported managed node initialization path, not by editing the host after deployment.
• Verify the live kubelet configuration shows rotation enabled.
Remediation of existing running cluster For an existing OKE cluster, the objective is to update the node initialization or node pool configuration so replacement nodes start with kubelet client certificate rotation enabled, then replace the current nodes so the corrected state is applied consistently across the node pool. Oracle documents that managed nodes can be cycled, terminated, and replaced, and that updated node pool properties apply to replacement worker nodes.
• Update the cloud-init initialization script or equivalent managed node configuration so rotateCertificates: true is applied.
• Roll the managed node pool so replacement nodes launch with the corrected setting.
• If the node pool does not use the required managed node customization, update the existing node pool or create a new node pool with the required configuration and migrate workloads.

A host-level change can be bypassed by the node’s initialization configuration and lost when the node is recycled or replaced.

Rule.title: Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that cluster administrative access in Oracle OKE is granted only to identities with a documented need for full cluster administration. In OKE, this review should cover Kubernetes ClusterRoleBinding assignments to the cluster-admin ClusterRole, OCI IAM users or groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, and any service accounts bound to cluster administrative permissions. Where administration is limited to a team, application, or namespace boundary, use a narrower authorization model instead of cluster admin access.

Rationale:
This setting enforces least privilege across the most sensitive OKE authorization paths.
Oracle documents that OCI IAM controls who can use OKE to manage clusters and obtain access to the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do with the Kubernetes API inside the cluster. Oracle also documents that Kubernetes RBAC rolebindings and clusterrolebindings can map roles and clusterroles to users or groups, including OCI IAM users and groups by OCID. Together, these OKE behaviors make it important to keep cluster-admin use exceptional, tightly bounded, and reviewable.</VulnDiscussion>

Review each ClusterRoleBinding identified by the audit that grants the Kubernetes cluster-admin ClusterRole, and determine whether the listed user, group, or service account still requires full cluster administrative access. In Oracle OKE, this review should also account for access granted through OCI IAM policies and Kubernetes RBAC mappings, because Oracle documents that IAM and the Kubernetes RBAC Authorizer work together to authorize Kubernetes operations. Where responsibilities are limited to a namespace, workload, or operational function, replace cluster administration with a narrower authorization model.
• Review each principal returned by the audit and confirm whether full cluster administrative access is still justified for that identity.
• For OCI IAM users or groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, remove unnecessary cluster-admin bindings and replace them with narrower Kubernetes RBAC permissions or an OCI IAM and RBAC model aligned to the approved operational need.
• For principals granted access through Kubernetes RBAC, replace unnecessary cluster-admin bindings with a lower-privilege Role, ClusterRole, or namespace RoleBinding that matches the approved operational need.
• Validate that the replacement access allows the user, group, or service account to perform its approved tasks before removing the original cluster-admin binding.
• Remove the unneeded ClusterRoleBinding only after the reduced privilege access has been confirmed to work as intended.
• Do not remove ClusterRoleBindings required for OKE cluster operations, Oracle managed add-ons, or approved administrative service accounts unless you have validated the operational impact.
Internal Only - General
• Review privilege OCI IAM groups separately, because OCI IAM controls access to manage OKE clusters and obtain access to the cluster control plane.
Where possible, first assign a lower privilege role, validate required access, and then remove the ClusterRoleBinding that grants cluster-admin:
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding [name]

Rule.title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that access to Kubernetes Secret objects in Oracle OKE is granted only to OCI IAM users or groups, Kubernetes users or groups, and service accounts with a defined operational or workload need. The review should cover OCI IAM access to the cluster, Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings, OCI IAM groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, workload identities, and service account permissions, with particular attention to permissions that allow get, list, or watch access to Secrets. Where access is needed, scope it as narrowly as possible, because OKE uses OCI IAM for cluster access and Kubernetes RBAC for fine grained cluster authorization.

Rationale:
This requirement reduces unnecessary exposure to one of the most sensitive resource types in an OKE cluster. Oracle documents that OCI IAM controls who can use OKE to manage clusters and access the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster. Oracle also documents that Kubernetes RBAC roles, clusterroles, rolebindings, and clusterrolebindings can be used to grant fine grained permissions to users and groups, including OCI IAM users and groups by OCID. Minimizing Secrets access therefore helps prevent broad read access from being granted through overlapping OCI IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and service account authorization paths.
For workloads, least privilege access should be applied to both Kubernetes service accounts and OCI IAM policies. OKE workload identity identifies a workload by the unique combination of cluster, namespace, and service account, and can be used to grant fine grained access to OCI resources. Excessive Secrets access combined with overprivileged workload identities can then expand a pod or node compromise beyond Kubernetes RBAC into OCI API access.</VulnDiscussion>

Start by reducing every access path that allows reading Kubernetes Secret objects in the OKE cluster. Start with OCI IAM access and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OCI IAM controls access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources such as Secrets. Then reduce unnecessary access in Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and workload identity policies, and replace broad permissions with the narrowest namespace or workload scope that still supports the required function.
• Remove or narrow OCI IAM and Kubernetes RBAC permissions that expose Secrets, and prefer namespace access over cluster scope wherever possible.
Internal Only - General
• Replace broad RBAC permissions on secrets with the smallest practical Role or ClusterRole, and remove unnecessary get, list, or watch access from users, groups, and service accounts.
• Reduce service account access to Secrets to only the workloads that require it, and tighten any related workload identity OCI IAM permissions to least privilege.
• Review broadly deployed workloads and privileged operational service accounts first, because their tokens and permissions can increase exposure if the workload or node is compromised.
• Remove stale OCI IAM group mappings or Kubernetes RBAC bindings that still place principals into groups with Secrets access.
• Validate that each remaining Secrets access path is tied to a documented operational or workload requirement, and flag any unnecessary access for removal.

Start by reviewing every path that can grant access to Kubernetes Secret objects in the OKE cluster. Start with OCI IAM access to the cluster and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls cluster authorization. Then review Kubernetes RBAC, service account permissions, and workload identities, because OKE can combine cluster access, Kubernetes RBAC, and OCI resource access through service account based workload identity.

Rule.title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole objects in Oracle OKE do not use wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups unless a documented administrative or platform requirement exists. The review should also include the RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects that assign those roles to users, groups, or service accounts, because OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do through the Kubernetes API inside the cluster.

Rationale:
This recommendation supports least privilege authorization in OKE Kubernetes RBAC.
Oracle documents that OCI IAM controls who can use OKE to manage clusters and obtain access to the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster.
Oracle also documents that Kubernetes RBAC roles, clusterroles, rolebindings, and clusterrolebindings can be used to grant specific permissions to users and groups, including OCI IAM users and groups by OCID. In that model, wildcard rules make the effective privilege set harder to predict, harder to review, and easier to overextend across current and future resources. The risk is higher for service accounts used by broadly deployed controllers or platform components, because those Kubernetes RBAC permissions can be exposed if the workload, pod, or node is compromised.</VulnDiscussion>

In OKE, this remediation should focus on customer managed RBAC objects, the bindings that assign them, OCI IAM users and groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, workload identities, and service accounts used by workloads or cluster components. OKE uses OCI IAM for access to OKE and the cluster control plane, and Kubernetes RBAC for authorization inside the cluster, so both access paths should be reviewed when excessive permissions are found.
• Replace wildcard values in custom Role and ClusterRole rules with the specific verbs, resources, and apiGroups the function actually requires.
• Reduce or remove any RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding that assign those wildcard roles more broadly than necessary, and prefer bindings limited to the required namespace where possible.
• Review OCI IAM users and groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, because those users and groups can receive wildcard permissions through rolebindings or clusterrolebindings.
• Review service accounts for broadly deployed controllers, storage drivers, ingress controllers, and other platform components first, and remove wildcard permissions that are not required for their runtime behavior.
• Distinguish customer managed roles from Oracle managed and Kubernetes system roles before making changes, and avoid modifying Oracle managed or Kubernetes system RBAC objects unless you intentionally want to change how a platform component operates.

• After narrowing the role definition, validate that the user, group, or service account can still perform its approved tasks, then remove the superseded wildcard role or binding.

Rule.title: Minimize access to create pods
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The ability to create Pods in OKE is a sensitive permission that should be limited to approved deployment and operational functions. In OKE, Pod creation is controlled through Kubernetes RBAC after OCI IAM allows access to the cluster control plane.
Because Pods run within a namespace, use a service account, and can carry workload permissions, Pod creation should be limited to the smallest practical namespace and workload boundary.

Rationale:
Creating a Pod can allow a principal to run code with the permissions of the service account assigned to that Pod. OKE uses Kubernetes service accounts for workloads, and Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do with the Kubernetes API inside the cluster. Those behaviors make Pod creation more than a routine write permission, because it can become a path to exercise Kubernetes API permissions indirectly through workload identity.
The risk can extend beyond Kubernetes RBAC into OCI access. With OKE workload identity, a workload is identified by the unique combination of cluster, namespace, and service account, allowing IAM policies to grant that workload access to OCI resources.
OKE pod security guidance also identifies higher risk Pod behaviors such as privileged execution and hostPath usage, which means the ability to create Pods can also expose host or node attack paths if security controls do not constrain the Pod spec.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Default service accounts in OKE should not be used as the active identity for ordinary application or automation workloads. If a Pod does not specify a service account, Kubernetes automatically assigns the namespace default service account, and that account can authenticate to the Kubernetes API through its mounted token. Workloads that need Kubernetes or OCI access should instead use an explicitly assigned, dedicated service account that matches the intended namespace, application, and permission boundary.

Rationale:
This supports least privilege at the workload identity layer by using a dedicated service account for each application, including workloads that need Kubernetes API access or OKE workload identity. This allows RBAC and workload identity to be limited to the specific resources and actions required by each application, instead of sharing one namespace identity across unrelated Pods.
The default service account is especially risky when Pods inherit it implicitly. In OKE, workloads are automatically assigned a service account if one is not specified, and service account tokens are automatically mounted unless token auto mounting is disabled. For workloads that need OCI access, OKE workload identity uses the unique combination of cluster, namespace, and service account to grant access to OCI resources, so relying on the default account makes it harder to isolate OCI permissions cleanly and increases the chance that multiple workloads share the same Kubernetes and OCI identity path.</VulnDiscussion>

Create dedicated service accounts for workloads that need Kubernetes API access or OKE workload identity, and update those workloads to explicitly set serviceAccountName rather than relying on the namespace default service account.
For workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access, disable service account token auto mounting and avoid using the default service account as the active workload identity. Also review the default service account in each namespace and ensure it is not bound to unnecessary RBAC permissions.
Modify the default service account in each application namespace to set:
automountServiceAccountToken: false
Then validate workload manifests, because a Pod automountServiceAccountToken setting can override the service account setting, and workloads that actually need Kubernetes API access must use an explicitly assigned service account instead of inheriting default.

kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken":
false}'

Rule.title: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Service account tokens in OKE should be mounted only for Pods that require Kubernetes API access or an explicitly configured workload identity flow. Rationale:
This setting is important because a mounted service account token is an authentication credential. Oracle documents that Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster, and that a service account binds pods in a workload to Kubernetes role permissions and grants access to Kubernetes resources.

The risk is higher when workload identity is involved. Rule.title: Minimize the admission of privileged containers
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize the admission of privileged containers in OKE by enforcing Pod Security Standards through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine, and restrict privileged workloads to only the limited system or platform namespaces that truly require them.

Clusters created with OKE use either the OCI CNI plugin or the flannel CNI plugin for pod networking, depending on the cluster network type and creation path. Oracle supports NetworkPolicy enforcement through Calico when using the OCI CNI plugin.
Oracle does not support using the Calico network policy engine with the flannel CNI plugin.
If the cluster uses the OCI CNI plugin, install and configure Calico network policy enforcement using Oracle’s documented process, then create the required namespace NetworkPolicies.
If the cluster uses flannel and NetworkPolicy enforcement is required, follow Oracle’s documented migration or replacement approach rather than installing Calico alongside flannel. Oracle notes that installing the Calico network policy engine alongside flannel can cause network issues and is not supported.

check.check-content:
Run the below command and review the NetworkPolicy objects created in the cluster.
This command will list all namespaces in your OKE cluster that have one or more NetworkPolicy objects defined:
Internal Only - General
echo -e "NAMESPACE\tNETWORKPOLICY_COUNT" && \
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l
| tr -d ' ')
if [ "$count" -gt 0 ]; then
echo -e "${ns}\t${count}"
fi
done
OR show namespaces that do not have Network Policies defined
echo -e "NAMESPACES_WITHOUT_NETWORKPOLICIES" && \
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
if ! kubectl get networkpolicy -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | grep -q
.; then
echo "$ns"
fi
done
Ensure that each workload namespace defined in the cluster has at least one Network Policy. Review system and platform namespaces separately, because they may require different network rules. Also confirm that NetworkPolicy enforcement is supported by the cluster networking configuration.

Rule.title: Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Secrets for OKE workloads are better exposed as mounted files than as environment variables. Kubernetes secrets can be consumed either way, and Oracle supports mounting secrets from OCI Vault into Kubernetes Pods through the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver.

Rationale:
Environment variable values can unintentionally appear in logs, while secrets mounted as volumes are instantiated as tmpfs volumes and are automatically removed from the node when the Pod is deleted. File based delivery also aligns with the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider model, which enables Kubernetes clusters to access secrets stored in OCI Vault and mount them into Pods through the Secrets Store CSI Driver.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Update workloads to consume secrets as mounted files instead of environment variables. Replace env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and envFrom[].secretRef usage with Kubernetes Secret volumes or the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, then update the application to read the secret from the mounted file path. This reduces the chance of secret values appearing in logs and aligns with the OCI Vault based file delivery pattern for OKE workloads.
Replace secret environment variables with mounted secret files and update the application to read from the mounted path.

check.check-content:
Review workload manifests and identify any Pod, Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, Job, or CronJob that exposes secrets through environment variables instead of mounted files. Check for both direct secret references through env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and bulk secret imports through envFrom[].secretRef, because either pattern exposes secret data as environment variables. Prefer workloads that consume secrets through mounted Secret volumes or file based delivery from OCI secrets integrations instead.
Run this command to list workloads that reference secrets through either environment-variable pattern:
Internal Only - General
kubectl get deploy,ds,sts,job,cronjob,pod -A -o json | jq -r '
.items[]
| .kind as $kind
| .metadata.namespace as $ns
| .metadata.name as $name
| (if $kind == "Pod" then .spec else .spec.template.spec end) as $spec
| select([ $spec.containers[]?, $spec.initContainers[]? ] |
any(.env[]?.valueFrom.secretKeyRef? or .envFrom[]?.secretRef?))
| "\($ns)\t\($kind)/\($name)"
'
• The command returns one line for each workload that exposes a Kubernetes Secret through an environment variable pattern.
Sample output:
default Deployment/web-app
apps StatefulSet/orders-api
logging DaemonSet/log-agent
batch Job/nightly-report
reports CronJob/monthly-export
Note: For this audit, no output is the preferred result, because it means no matching workloads were found exposing Secrets as environment variables

Rule.title: Consider external secret storage
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>External secret storage for OKE means keeping application secrets outside native Kubernetes Secret objects and retrieving them from a managed service such as OCI Vault when workloads need them. This approach lets OKE workloads consume secrets through integrations such as the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, instead of relying only on Kubernetes to store and distribute sensitive values.

Rationale:
Storing sensitive credentials outside Kubernetes reduces dependence on Secret objects stored inside the cluster and shifts lifecycle functions such as encryption, access control, rotation, and audit to a dedicated secrets service. In OKE, Pods can retrieve secrets from OCI Vault by using OCI IAM access through OKE workload identity, and the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider can mount those values into Pods as files through the Secrets Store CSI Driver. This model supports centralized secret lifecycle management and tighter secret to workload access control than broadly distributing static values through Kubernetes manifests.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Move sensitive application secrets out of native Kubernetes Secret objects and into an external store such as OCI Vault. Then update OKE workloads to retrieve those secrets through the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, using OCI IAM access through OKE workload identity. This shifts encryption, access control, rotation, and auditing to OCI instead of leaving those functions primarily in Secret objects stored inside the cluster.
• Create the required secrets in OCI Vault and define workload access with least privilege OCI IAM policies.
• Install and configure the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider and the Secrets Store CSI Driver for OKE.
• Update workload manifests to mount external secrets through a SecretProviderClass instead of reading only native Kubernetes Secret objects.
• Enable rotation and update the application to read secrets from the mounted path so secret lifecycle management is handled centrally in OCI.
• Move secrets to OCI Vault, mount them into Pods, and limit access with OKE workload identity.

check.check-content:
Review the OKE cluster’s secrets architecture and verify that required workloads use an external secrets store such as OCI Vault instead of relying only on native Kubernetes Secret objects. The audit should confirm both the integration path and the workload access model, because external secret storage in OKE typically depends on the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider, the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and OCI IAM access through OKE workload identity.
• Identify workloads that still consume sensitive credentials from native Kubernetes Secrets and determine which of those should be moved to OCI Vault.
• Confirm the external secret integration components are in use, including the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider and Secrets Store CSI Driver, and verify that workloads reference a SecretProviderClass where external secrets are mounted as files.
Internal Only - General
• Verify workload access is limited through OKE workload identity so each workload can retrieve only the secrets it is authorized to read.
• Check whether rotation, access control, and audit requirements are being handled in the external store rather than duplicated through static secret values embedded in Kubernetes manifests or long lived native Secret objects.

Rule.title: Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Namespaces create administrative boundaries in OKE by dividing a cluster into logical partitions for teams, applications, or tenants. They are a core building block for multi tenancy, and several controls used to separate workloads, including quotas, network policies, and service accounts, apply to namespaces.

Rationale:
Namespaces matter operationally because many access and governance controls in Kubernetes and OKE can be applied by namespace. Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects are used to delegate permissions within a namespace, and OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster.
That allows platform teams to grant administrative access to only the namespaces a team or workload should manage, rather than granting broad cluster permissions.
The namespace boundary becomes stronger when it is combined with namespace specific resource and traffic controls. ResourceQuota and LimitRange can constrain CPU, memory, and object consumption within a namespace, while network policies can restrict Pod to Pod communication and support a least privilege model between tenant or application namespaces. A namespace alone is still only a logical grouping construct, so effective administrative separation depends on pairing it with RBAC, OCI IAM access design, quotas, service accounts, and network isolation.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Create separate namespaces for teams, applications, or environments that require their own administrative boundary, and move workloads out of the default namespace into that managed namespace structure. Make the namespace boundary meaningful by limiting access to the intended namespaces, applying namespace level governance such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies, and reducing broad cluster permissions that bypass the intended separation model. When stronger isolation is required for mutually untrusted workloads, use separate clusters rather than relying on namespaces alone.
• Create dedicated namespaces for each team, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary.
• Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespaces.
• Rebind access with namespace specific Role and RoleBinding objects and, where used, map OCI IAM users or groups to Kubernetes RBAC permissions that are limited to the intended namespaces.
Internal Only - General
• Apply ResourceQuota, LimitRange, service accounts, and network policies to reinforce namespace level governance and traffic separation.
• Remove unused namespaces and reduce unnecessary broad cluster permissions or OCI IAM access that bypass the intended namespace boundary.
Create dedicated namespaces, move workloads out of default, limit access by namespace, and apply quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies to enforce the administrative boundary.

check.check-content:
Verify that namespaces are present and are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for teams, applications, or environments in the OKE cluster. Namespaces are the core logical partition for multi tenancy, and they should be paired with namespace specific access controls and namespace level governance such as quotas, limits, and network policies. A namespace should be considered adequately administered only when it has a clear workload or team purpose, appropriately limited access, and the namespace level controls required for that use case.
Internal Only - General
• List all namespaces and confirm each has a defined administrative, application, or environment purpose. Namespaces are the base partitioning construct for multi tenancy in OKE.
• Verify that user and workload access is limited to the intended namespaces through Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects and, where used, OCI IAM groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, rather than broad cluster grants.
OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, and Kubernetes RBAC to control authorization inside the cluster.
• Review whether namespace level controls such as ResourceQuota, LimitRange, service accounts, and network policies are applied where required to support separation, resource governance, and Pod to Pod traffic restrictions.
• Confirm that broad cluster access is limited to identities that truly require it, because namespace boundaries alone do not prevent cross tenant or cross workload access.
Inventory checks for OKE Clusters:
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get rolebindings,roles -A
kubectl get clusterrolebindings,clusterroles
kubectl get resourcequota,limitrange,networkpolicy -A
oci iam policy list --compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID
Note: Review OCI IAM policies and group membership for access to OKE and the cluster control plane, then review Kubernetes RBAC objects to confirm what those authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster.

Rule.title: Apply securityContext controls to pods and containers
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers. For OKE workloads, securityContext controls should be used with Pod Security Admission or an equivalent admission policy so pods and containers run with only the operating system privileges they require.

Rationale:
A security context defines the operating system security settings (uid, gid, capabilities, SELinux role, etc..) applied to a container. When designing your containers and pods, make sure that you configure the security context for your pods, containers, and volumes. A security context is a property defined in the deployment yaml. It controls the security parameters that will be assigned to the pod/container/volume. There are two levels of security context: pod level security context, and container level security context. In OKE, PodSecurity is a supported admission controller, and Oracle guidance points to Pod Security Standards and the PodSecurity admission controller for enforcing pod security behavior at admission time.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Use securityContext settings in workload manifests and enforce the required Pod Security Standard with Pod Security Admission or an equivalent admission policy. Avoid using legacy PodSecurityPolicy manifests for current OKE clusters.
For normal application workloads, configure pod and container securityContext settings that align to the intended security level. Common settings include running as a non root user, disabling privilege escalation, dropping unnecessary Linux capabilities, restricting host namespace use, and setting read only root filesystems where the application supports it.
securityContext:
runAsNonRoot: true
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
capabilities:
drop:
- ALL
• Label workload namespaces to enforce the required Pod Security Standard.
kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --
overwrite
• Add warn and audit labels during rollout if you want visibility into violations before or alongside enforcement.
kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted --
overwrite
kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted --
overwrite
• Redeploy affected workloads after manifest changes so replacement pods are evaluated under the enforced namespace policy. Review system namespaces separately because platform components can require different security settings.
Internal Only - General

check.check-content:
Review the pod definitions in your cluster and verify that you have security contexts defined as appropriate.
Here is a key compliance check in OKE (Oracle Kubernetes Engine) to ensure all Pods define a securityContext at either the pod or container level:

"NAMESPACE\tPOD\tHAS_POD_SECURITY_CONTEXT\tHAS_CONTAINER_SECURITY_CONTEXT" &&
\
kubectl get pods -A -o json \
| jq -r '
.items[]
| .metadata.namespace as $ns
| .metadata.name as $pod
| (.spec.securityContext != null) as $hasPodSC
| ([(.spec.containers[]?.securityContext != null)] | any) as
$hasContainerSC
| [$ns, $pod, $hasPodSC, $hasContainerSC] | @tsv
'

• HAS_CONTAINER_SECURITY_CONTEXT: verifies if any container in the pod defines.securityContext
