Rule.title: The default namespace should not be used
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. In OKE, namespaces are a primary logical partition for organizing workloads and supporting multi tenancy in a shared cluster.

Rationale:
Least privilege administration in OKE depends on using namespaces as intentional operational boundaries. Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects apply within a namespace, and OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster. When workloads remain in default, access delegation, ownership boundaries, and namespace level governance become harder to separate cleanly.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Move user workloads out of the default namespace and place them in dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. In OKE, namespaces are the core logical partition for multi tenancy, but they only become meaningful administrative boundaries when they are paired with namespace level access, service accounts, quotas, limits, and network policies. Because namespaced objects are created in default when no namespace is specified, remediation should address both existing workloads and the deployment process that created them there.
• Create dedicated namespaces for each team, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary.
• Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespaces.
• Update manifests, Helm values, GitOps definitions, and pipeline defaults so namespaced resources explicitly set metadata.namespace and are not created in default by omission.
• Rebind access with namespace level Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding objects and, where OCI IAM users or groups are mapped to Kubernetes RBAC, limit the resulting Kubernetes permissions to the intended namespaces.
• Apply namespace level governance such as ResourceQuota, LimitRange, dedicated service accounts, and network policies so the namespace boundary supports resource control, identity separation, and Pod to Pod traffic isolation.
Internal Only - General
• Remove unnecessary user workloads and broad operational access from default, and use separate clusters rather than namespaces alone when stronger isolation is required for less trusted workloads.
Move workloads out of default, enforce explicit namespaces in deployment workflows, and bind access and governance controls to the target namespaces.

check.check-content:
Review the OKE cluster and verify that the default namespace is not being used for normal application administration or routine workload placement. Objects that do not explicitly specify a namespace are created in default, so the audit should confirm that teams, applications, and environments are instead using dedicated namespaces that align with namespace level access control, quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies. Namespaces are a logical administrative boundary in OKE, so the goal is to confirm that user workloads are intentionally placed outside default and governed through namespace level controls.
• Inventory the default namespace and identify any user-managed Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ServiceAccounts, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, Ingresses, Roles, RoleBindings, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, or NetworkPolicies that still exist there.
Internal Only - General
kubectl get
pod,svc,configmap,secret,serviceaccount,deploy,statefulset,daemonset,job,cron
job,ingress,role,rolebinding,resourcequota,limitrange,networkpolicy -n
default
• Verify that access is not effectively centered on default. Review Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding assignments for that namespace and review OCI IAM policies and group membership for access to OKE and the cluster control plane.
OKE uses OCI IAM for cluster access and Kubernetes RBAC for authorization inside the cluster.
• Confirm that user workloads have been placed into dedicated namespaces that reflect team, application, or environment boundaries, and that namespace level controls such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies are applied where required. Those controls are what make a namespace an actual administrative boundary instead of just a label.
• Check whether the namespace design reduces shared administrative access and naming sprawl. OKE supports namespace based organization with Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, quotas, and network policies used to govern resources inside the cluster.
• Inventory the default namespace, identify user workloads still running there, and confirm access and governance are instead aligned to dedicated namespaces.

Rule.title: Ensure image vulnerability scanning uses OCIR or a third party provider
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Container image vulnerability scanning helps strengthen the security of OKE workloads by identifying known software weaknesses in the images those workloads run. This supports a more secure software supply chain and helps reduce the chance that vulnerable images are promoted into Kubernetes environments.

Rationale:
Oracle Container Registry can scan images in a repository for security vulnerabilities published in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures database, using the OCI Vulnerability Scanning service. When image scanning is enabled for a repository, newly pushed images are scanned, existing images are scanned based on the configured scan target behavior, and images are automatically rescanned when new vulnerabilities are added to the CVE database.
Vulnerabilities in container image software packages can be exploited to compromise workloads and potentially gain unauthorized access to cluster, node, or connected cloud resources. OCIR and approved third party tools can scan container images for known vulnerabilities.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Enable image vulnerability scanning for OCIR repositories that supply container images to OKE workloads, or use an approved third party image scanning provider that produces equivalent vulnerability findings before image promotion and deployment. For OCIR, configure OCI Vulnerability Scanning with a container scan recipe and target for the repositories that store OKE images.
Identify the OCIR repositories and compartments that provide images to OKE workloads. This establishes which repositories must be included in the scanning coverage.
Configure OCI Vulnerability Scanning for the required repositories. Create a container image scan recipe in the compartment that will manage the scan configuration.
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan recipe create --display-name
$SCAN_RECIPE_NAME --compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID --scan-settings
'{"scanLevel":"STANDARD"}'
Generate the target registry JSON template and update it for the OCIR repositories that must be scanned.
Internal Only - General
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan target create --generate-param-
json-input target-registry > target-registry.json
Create a container scan target that applies the scan recipe to the selected OCIR repositories.
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan target create --compartment-id
$COMPARTMENT_ID --container-scan-recipe-id $CONTAINER_SCAN_RECIPE_OCID --
target-registry file://target-registry.json
Review vulnerability findings and rebuild, replace, or prevent deployment of images with unacceptable risk before they are used by OKE workloads. This makes the control operational rather than leaving findings unaddressed.

check.check-content:
Verify that image vulnerability scanning is enabled for repositories that store images used by OKE workloads. For images stored in OCIR, review the Container Registry image scanner or OCI Vulnerability Scanning container scan targets and scan results. If a third party scanner is used instead, obtain equivalent evidence that images deployed to OKE are scanned and that findings are available for review.
Checks the container scan targets in the compartment. Use it to confirm that OCIR repositories used by OKE workloads are included in a Vulnerability Scanning target:
Internal Only - General
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan target list --compartment-id
$COMPARTMENT_ID --all
• Expected output: JSON showing container scan targets. In that object, look for display-name, lifecycle-state, compartment-id, container-scan- recipe-id, and target-registry to confirm which OCIR repositories are covered.
Checks the container scan recipes in the compartment. Use it to confirm the scan settings applied by the scan target:
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan recipe list --compartment-id
$COMPARTMENT_ID --all
• Expected output: JSON showing container scan recipes. In that object, look for display-name, lifecycle-state, scan-settings, and id to confirm the recipe used by the scan target.
Checks the container image scan results. Use it to confirm scan findings exist for images in covered OCIR repositories:
oci vulnerability-scanning container scan result list --compartment-id
$COMPARTMENT_ID --all
• Expected output: JSON showing scan reports for container images. Review the image path, risk level, lifecycle state, and scan timing to confirm that images used by OKE workloads are being scanned and findings are available for review.

Rule.title: Restrict OKE and Kubernetes API access to required users
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Restrict access to OKE and Kubernetes API operations to only authorized OCI IAM users, groups, and Kubernetes service accounts. Access should be limited based on the user’s required administrative, operational, or workload function.

Rationale:
Excessive access to OKE or the Kubernetes API can allow unauthorized users or service accounts to create, modify, or delete clusters, node pools, workloads, secrets, and other Kubernetes resources. Oracle documents that OCI IAM controls who can manage OKE resources and access the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls what authenticated users and service accounts can do inside the cluster.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
By default, users are not assigned any Kubernetes RBAC roles (or clusterroles) by default. So before attempting to create a new role (or clusterrole), you must be assigned an appropriately privileged role (or clusterrole). A number of such roles and clusterroles are always created by default, including the cluster-admin clusterrole (for a full list, see Default Roles and Role Bindings in the Kubernetes documentation). The cluster- admin clusterrole essentially confers super-user privileges. A user granted the cluster- admin clusterrole can perform any operation across all namespaces in a given cluster.
Remove or reduce OCI IAM policies that grant unnecessary OKE permissions, and use Kubernetes RBAC roles and rolebindings to grant only the required Kubernetes API permissions inside the cluster. Avoid granting cluster-admin unless full cluster administration is required. Review high privilege service accounts and automation identities separately before making changes to avoid disrupting required platform operations.

check.check-content:
For most operations on Kubernetes clusters created and managed by Container Engine for Kubernetes, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Identity and Access Management (IAM) provides access control. A user's permissions to access clusters comes from the groups to which they belong. The permissions for a group are defined by policies. Policies define what actions members of a group can perform, and in which compartments.
Users can then access clusters and perform operations based on the policies set for the groups they are members of.
IAM provides control over:
• whether a user can create or delete clusters
• whether a user can add, remove, or modify node pools
• which Kubernetes object create/delete/view operations a user can perform on all clusters within a compartment or tenancy
• See Policy Configuration for Cluster Creation and Deployment.
Internal Only - General In addition to IAM, the Kubernetes RBAC Authorizer can enforce additional access control for users on specific clusters via Kubernetes RBAC roles and clusterroles. A Kubernetes RBAC role is a collection of permissions. For example, a role might include read permission on pods and list permission for pods. A Kubernetes RBAC clusterrole is just like a role, but can be used anywhere in the cluster. A Kubernetes RBAC rolebinding maps a role to a user or set of users, granting that role's permissions to those users for resources in that namespace. Similarly, a Kubernetes RBAC clusterrolebinding maps a clusterrole to a user or set of users, granting that clusterrole's permissions to those users for cluster resources.
Review OCI IAM policies that grant access to OKE resources.
oci iam policy list --compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID --all
Review Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings that grant access inside the cluster.
kubectl get rolebindings,roles -A
kubectl get clusterrolebindings,clusterroles
Confirm that each OCI IAM policy, RoleBinding, and ClusterRoleBinding is tied to a documented administrative, operational, or workload requirement.

Rule.title: Restrict OCIR access for OKE workloads to required image pulls
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Restricting OCIR access for OKE workload image pulls helps ensure that the identities used to retrieve workload images can pull required container images without also receiving broader registry visibility, push, delete, or repository management access. In OKE, this applies to the OCI IAM users, groups, cluster policies, and Kubernetes imagePullSecrets used to pull images from private OCIR repositories.

Rationale:
The OKE runtime image pull path for private OCIR images requires registry credentials and repository access sufficient to pull image layers and manifests. Oracle documents that images pulled from OCIR during Kubernetes deployment require a Docker registry secret containing OCI credentials, and the workload manifest must reference that secret through imagePullSecrets. A pull-only policy is therefore a closer least privilege match for runtime image pulls because it supports image retrieval without also granting repository push, delete, visibility, or management actions.
A broader OCIR policy is unnecessary for workload image pulls because Oracle documents separate policy levels for inspecting repositories, pulling images, pushing images, and managing repositories. For image pull access, Oracle documents the read repos permission as the policy level that allows pulling images from Container Registry.
Broader policies such as manage repos can allow push, repository deletion, or repository metadata changes, which are useful for administrators or CI/CD publishers but are not required just to start OKE workloads from private OCIR images. Restricting runtime identities to pull-only permissions therefore reduces unnecessary registry exposure while still preserving the permissions required for image retrieval.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes(OKE) Benchmark

fixtext.+content:
Enforce pull-only OCIR access for OKE workload image pull identities by limiting the OCI IAM users, groups, cluster policies, and imagePullSecrets used to retrieve private images. The runtime pull path should allow only the repository access required to pull image layers and manifests. Broader permissions that allow pushing images, deleting repositories, changing repository visibility, or managing repository metadata are not required just to start workloads.
• Identify the OCI identities, groups, policies, and imagePullSecrets used by OKE workloads to pull private OCIR images.
• Remove broader OCIR policies from runtime image pull identities. Avoid granting manage repos to identities that only need image pull access.
• Replace broad repository access with read repos for the required repositories or compartments. Oracle documents read repos as the policy level that allows pulling images from Container Registry.
• Allow group <image-puller-group> to read repos in compartment <compartment-name>
• Where possible, limit access to the required repositories by repository name condition.
• Allow group <image-puller-group> to read repos in compartment <compartment-name> where all { target.repo.name=/app-prefix*/ }
• Remove or replace policies that add push, delete, or repository management access unless there is a documented operational need.

Rule.title: Allow only approved container registries for images used by OKE workloads
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Allowing only approved container registries for images used by OKE workloads helps reduce supply chain risk by limiting where workloads can source their images. This creates a controlled image origin model in which clusters admit workloads only from trusted registries and can pair that control with OCIR image signature verification before containers are allowed to run.

Rationale:
A practical way to enforce this control in OKE is through admission controls that evaluate Kubernetes API requests before the requested change is persisted. Those policies can validate image source rules, verify signatures, and reject deployments that do not meet the required trust conditions. For images stored in OCIR, OKE supports image verification policies that allow deployment only when images are signed with specified master encryption keys from OCI Vault. This makes the registry restriction more than a naming convention and turns it into an admission control point tied to trusted publishers and approved image sources.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads helps isolate OCI permissions by application, job, or trust boundary instead of sharing a single identity across multiple workloads. This supports more controlled access to OCI services and reduces the security impact if one workload is compromised or misconfigured.

Rationale:
A workload that needs OCI access should run with a Kubernetes service account that is used with OKE workload identity, and that identity model should be created for each unique permission set an application needs. OKE workload identity uses the unique combination of cluster, namespace, and service account to authorize workload access to OCI resources through OCI IAM policies. Using a dedicated service account per workload or per permission boundary prevents unrelated pods in the same namespace from inheriting the same OCI access and aligns permissions more closely to the actual application function.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Use customer managed KMS keys for OKE envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using customer managed OCI Vault keys for OKE Kubernetes secrets encryption adds a customer managed protection layer for Kubernetes secrets stored through the Kubernetes API. This strengthens data at rest protection while allowing organizations to manage key ownership, rotation, policy, and audit visibility for the key used to protect secret data.

Rationale:
Envelope encryption adds a second encryption layer to Kubernetes secrets stored through the OKE control plane. Secret data is encrypted with a unique data encryption key, and that data encryption key is then encrypted with a master encryption key stored in OCI Vault before the object is persisted in etcd. This means the secret is stored in ciphertext in the backing datastore and is decrypted only through the Kubernetes API server path, which strengthens protection beyond the underlying storage encryption used for etcd.
In the current OKE model, envelope encryption protects Kubernetes secrets in etcd by using a data encryption key and a master encryption key. A customer managed OCI Vault key gives the customer direct control over key selection, rotation, audit visibility, and key lifecycle for the key that protects those data encryption keys.</VulnDiscussion>

OKE does not allow you to enable customer managed Kubernetes secrets encryption on an existing cluster after creation. Oracle documents that this option is selected when creating a new cluster through the Custom Create workflow or with the OCI CLI by specifying the Vault key OCID.
• After the new cluster is created, the key must remain enabled and accessible.
Disabling, deleting, or breaking access to the associated key can place the cluster in a degraded or unrecoverable state.

• Create the required IAM policy so the OKE cluster can use the key. Oracle documents either an any-user policy with request.principal.type = 'cluster' and the target key OCID, or a dynamic group policy for clusters that need access to the key.

--name $CLUSTER_NAME \
--compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID \
--vcn-id $VCN_OCID \
--kubernetes-version $KUBERNETES_VERSION \
--kms-key-id $KEY_OCID

Rule.title: Restrict OKE control plane endpoint access using private endpoints or approved CIDRs
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation is about reducing exposure of the Kubernetes API server without necessarily making it private only. The intended end state is that the OKE Kubernetes API endpoint is placed behind a private endpoint where possible, or if a public IP address is assigned, access is limited to approved source CIDRs through OCI network security rules. This keeps the control plane reachable for approved administration paths while lowering unnecessary internet exposure.

Rationale:
OKE exposes the Kubernetes API through an endpoint hosted in a subnet of the cluster VCN. The Kubernetes API endpoint subnet can be private or public, and if a public subnet is used, the endpoint can optionally be assigned a public IP address. Access to the Kubernetes API endpoint subnet is controlled with network security groups or security lists. If the endpoint is private, access is limited to networks that can reach the VCN, such as connected subnets, peered VCNs, FastConnect, VPN, or bastion based administration paths. If the endpoint has a public IP address, the endpoint can be reached from the internet unless the endpoint subnet’s security rules restrict TCP/6443 to approved source CIDRs.
Restricting access to an authorized network can provide additional security benefits for your container cluster, including:
• Better protection from outsider attacks: Restricting the Kubernetes API endpoint to approved CIDRs or private network paths provides an additional layer of security by limiting external access to a specific set of addresses you designate, such as those that originate from your premises. This helps protect access to your cluster in the case of a vulnerability in the cluster's authentication or authorization mechanism.
• Better protection from insider attacks: Restricting endpoint access helps protect your cluster from accidental leaks of cluster access credentials from your company's premises. Leaked credentials used from outside approved network paths or approved CIDR ranges are still denied network access.
Internal Only - General</VulnDiscussion>

The Kubernetes API endpoint is hosted in a VCN subnet, and Oracle recommends using network security groups or security lists to control access to that subnet.
For new clusters, place the Kubernetes API endpoint in a private subnet when internet access to the API endpoint is not required.

--name $CLUSTER_NAME \
--compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID \
--vcn-id $VCN_OCID \
--kubernetes-version $KUBERNETES_VERSION \
--endpoint-subnet-id $PRIVATE_ENDPOINT_SUBNET_OCID \
--endpoint-public-ip-enabled false

Do not leave Kubernetes API endpoint access open to 0.0.0.0/0 unless there is a documented and approved requirement.
If an existing cluster uses a public Kubernetes API endpoint and a private endpoint is required, create or move to an OKE cluster design that places the API endpoint in a private subnet, then update kubeconfig access paths to use the private endpoint through approved network connectivity such as bastion, VPN, FastConnect, or peered VCN access.

Rule.title: Enable private OKE control plane access and disable public IP access
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation is the strict private access version of API endpoint hardening. The intended end state is that the Kubernetes API server is reachable only from inside the cluster VCN or from a connected private network, and there is no internet-reachable public API endpoint at all. This is a pure control plane exposure decision.

Rationale:
In OKE, the Kubernetes API endpoint is hosted in a subnet of the cluster VCN. The endpoint is always assigned a private IP address, and if the endpoint is placed in a public subnet, it can optionally be assigned a public IP address. For private control plane access, place the Kubernetes API endpoint in a private subnet and do not assign a public IP address. Administration from outside the VCN must use a private connectivity path, such as peered VCN access, VPN, FastConnect, or a bastion.
If the Kubernetes API endpoint has no public IP address, internet based kubectl access is not available. Access is governed by the endpoint subnet route rules, security lists, and network security groups. If public IP access is disabled, approved administrators and automation must reach the private endpoint through an allowed network path.
Although Kubernetes API requires an authorized token to perform sensitive actions, a vulnerability could potentially expose the Kubernetes API publicly with unrestricted access. Additionally, an attacker may be able to identify the current cluster and Kubernetes API version and determine whether it is vulnerable to an attack. Unless required, disabling public IP access will help prevent such threats, and require the attacker to be on the VCN or an approved connected network to perform any attack on the Kubernetes API.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This recommendation is about the data plane, not the control plane. It means worker nodes are placed in private subnets and are not intended to have direct public internet exposure. In the common pattern, nodes run in private subnets while internet-facing ingress resources are placed in public subnets. This changes where compute runs and how node traffic exits the VCN, but it does not by itself determine whether the Kubernetes API endpoint is public, private, or both.

Rationale:
OKE worker nodes are created with public or private IP addresses according to whether public or private subnets are specified when defining node pools. Placing nodes in private subnets reduces direct reachability of the worker instances and gives tighter control over egress paths. At the same time, those nodes still need access to required services such as OCIR for image pulls, and that access must be provided through a NAT gateway, service gateway, or other required private network path. In a fully private cluster design with no outbound internet access, the Kubernetes API endpoint and supporting OCI services must remain reachable through private connectivity, route rules, and security rules that support node registration, image pulls, and required workload operations.</VulnDiscussion>

If outbound access is required for image pulls or OCI API calls, provide it through a NAT gateway, service gateway, or the required private network path instead.

• Ensure the replacement subnets prohibit public IP assignment on VNICs, so new worker instances are launched without public IPs.
• Ensure the route tables for those subnets do not send 0.0.0.0/0 directly to an Internet Gateway. If internet egress is needed, route it through a NAT gateway or use a service gateway for supported OCI service access. OCIR image pulls and other required service access must remain available through the approved private egress design.

Rule.title: Ensure Network Policy is Enabled and set as appropriate
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Implementing Kubernetes NetworkPolicies in an Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster is a critical security measure for controlling and segregating Pod to Pod communication. By default, all pods in a Kubernetes cluster can freely communicate with each other, which increases the risk of lateral movement if a single workload is compromised. Enforcing network policies allows administrators to explicitly define which pods or namespaces can communicate, ensuring that workloads are properly isolated based on function, sensitivity, or compliance requirements. This segregation helps contain potential security breaches, limits unauthorized data access between applications, and supports the principle of least privilege in network communication, strengthening the overall security posture and reducing the attack surface within the OKE environment.
Configure NetworkPolicy enforcement and define NetworkPolicy resources to restrict Pod to Pod traffic within a cluster and segregate workloads.

Rationale:
By default, all pod to pod traffic within a cluster is allowed. NetworkPolicy creates a pod level firewall that can be used to restrict traffic between sources. Pod traffic is restricted by having a NetworkPolicy that selects it through the use of labels. Once there is any NetworkPolicy in a namespace selecting a particular pod, that pod will reject any connections that are not allowed by any NetworkPolicy. Other pods in the namespace that are not selected by any NetworkPolicy will continue to accept all traffic.
NetworkPolicies are managed via the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API and enforced by a network plugin, so simply creating the resource without a compatible network plugin to implement it will have no effect. OKE supports NetworkPolicy enforcement through integration with the Calico network policy engine when using the OCI CNI plugin. OKE does not support using the Calico network policy engine with the flannel CNI plugin.</VulnDiscussion>

For OKE, do not use an isNetworkPolicyEnabled cluster flag. Configure NetworkPolicy enforcement by using a supported enforcement solution and then create the required Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources.
If the cluster uses the OCI CNI plugin, install and configure the Calico network policy engine using Oracle’s documented process, then apply NetworkPolicy resources to workload namespaces.
If the cluster uses flannel and NetworkPolicy enforcement is required, follow Oracle’s documented approach to replace flannel with Calico for new nodes, or create a replacement cluster design that supports the required policy enforcement. Do not install Calico alongside flannel.
• Define namespace level NetworkPolicies after enforcement is available, and apply a restrictive default policy to each workload namespace where required.
• Add allow rules for required traffic and create specific NetworkPolicy resources to allow communication only between approved pods or namespaces.
Apply a Default Deny All Policy. Add specific policies for authorized communication by defining NetworkPolicy manifests that explicitly allow required traffic between trusted workloads, services, or namespaces.

Below is a command line statement to check whether NetworkPolicies are configured in your Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster:
echo -e "NAMESPACE\tNETWORK_POLICY_COUNT" && \
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l
| tr -d ' ')
echo -e "${ns}\t${count}"
done

default 2
kube-node-lease 3
kube-public 5
kube-system 0
A count of 0 means no NetworkPolicy objects exist in that namespace and pods that are not selected by any NetworkPolicy continue to accept all traffic.
A count greater than 0 means network policies are defined and applied, helping isolate and protect workloads.

.items[]
| select(
(.metadata.name | test("calico"; "i"))
or
([.spec.containers[]?.image] | join(" ") | test("calico"; "i"))
)
| "\(.metadata.namespace)\t\(.metadata.name)\t\(.status.phase)"
'

oci ce cluster list-addons --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID

Rule.title: Use TLS certificates on OKE load balancer listeners for encrypted client connections
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using TLS certificates on OKE load balancer listeners protects client to load balancer traffic in transit by presenting a trusted server certificate and negotiating encrypted HTTPS or TLS connections at the listener. In OKE, this commonly means configuring TLS on an OCI Load Balancer created for Kubernetes Service resources, or configuring HTTPS/TLS on OCI native ingress controller listeners so externally exposed application entry points do not rely on unencrypted HTTP.

Rationale:
OKE supports TLS configuration on the primary load balancer paths used for exposed workloads. For Kubernetes Services of type LoadBalancer, OCI Load Balancer listeners can terminate SSL/TLS using Kubernetes secrets or OCI Certificates service based certificate configuration. For OCI native ingress controller resources, HTTPS/TLS listeners can be configured using either a Kubernetes secret that allows the ingress controller to obtain a certificate from OCI Certificates, or a certificate OCID that references a certificate already created in OCI Certificates.
This matters because the listener is the point where the client session is negotiated, the certificate is presented, and encrypted traffic is established before requests are forwarded to targets. OKE also supports backend TLS where the design requires encryption between the load balancer and worker nodes or pods, so requiring certificates on client facing load balancer listeners is the baseline control for securing the external client connection path.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure every client facing OKE load balancer listener to use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate so client to load balancer traffic is encrypted in transit. For OCI Load Balancer backed Service resources, configure SSL/TLS listener ports and associate a TLS certificate using Kubernetes secrets or OCI Certificates based configuration. For OCI native ingress controller resources, configure HTTPS/TLS listeners and associate the required Kubernetes secret or certificate OCID. If the design requires encryption beyond the load balancer, implement backend TLS separately because listener TLS alone protects only the client facing connection.
• Add a valid certificate to each client facing OCI Load Balancer or OCI native ingress controller listener that should serve encrypted traffic.
• For OCI Load Balancer services, set service.beta.kubernetes.io/oci- load-balancer-ssl-ports to the required listener ports and configure the appropriate TLS certificate source.
• For OCI native ingress controller resources, configure HTTPS listeners and associate the required certificate source with the listener configuration.
• Replace or renew invalid certificates and implement backend TLS separately where backend encryption is required.
